title: Next.js Server Actions: RPC over the wire

progressiveExplaining.eli5: A restaurant where the guest writes a note, folds it into a little paper plane, and it flies back to the kitchen; the kitchen cooks and the finished dish appears on the table. The guest never sees the kitchen, never talks to the chef directly — but the order is placed and the meal arrives. A Server Action is that paper plane: a function that looks local, runs in the kitchen, and returns the finished result to the table.
progressiveExplaining.junior: With 'use server' at the top of a file (or inline in a server component), you can define functions that run on the server but are called from the client: async function createPost(formData) { 'use server'; await db.insert(...); revalidatePath('/'); }. Use them in <form action={createPost}> or call them directly from event handlers in Client Components (passing the imported server function as a prop). The framework serializes arguments and return values over the wire. Forms get a progressive enhancement bonus: if JavaScript fails to load, the form still submits via a plain POST.
progressiveExplaining.senior: Architecturally, Server Actions are the App Router's sanctioned RPC layer: they let you mutate server-side state (database, files, cache) without writing an API route, and they integrate with the data cache via revalidatePath/revalidateTag. The security boundary is critical: actions are POST endpoints with CSRF protection built into the protocol (the action ID + origin checks), and since they execute server-side with your privileges, every argument must be validated server-side — never trust serialized client input. They invert the old mental model of 'client mutates via API, then refetches'; the mutation and the refresh are one round trip.
progressiveExplaining.underTheHood: Each 'use server' function is compiled into a POST endpoint keyed by an action ID. The client reference is a stub that serializes the call (arguments via the React Flight serialization format — including FormData natively) into a POST request to the page's route or a dedicated action route. The server validates the origin (the Action-Submission-Origin header), deserializes arguments with the matching server reference, executes the function, and returns serialized JSX (for re-rendered trees) or a plain value. State updates and revalidatePath calls are applied server-side, and the client merges the returned Flight payload into the React tree — which is why a form action can update both data and UI in one round trip. Nested server actions inside Server Components are extracted and compiled the same way.

codeComparison.title: Client-side fetch to an API route vs a Server Action
codeComparison.summary: The fetch-to-API approach splits mutation and cache invalidation across two endpoints; a Server Action mutates and revalidates in one compiled RPC call.

interviewGotchas.question: What security concerns are specific to Server Actions, and how does Next.js mitigate them?
interviewGotchas.contextIntro: This is the most important follow-up in production interviews — actions execute server-side with your privileges, so the security model matters more than the syntax.
interviewGotchas.detailedAnswer: Server Actions are effectively POST endpoints, so they inherit endpoint security requirements: authenticate and authorize every action, and validate all inputs server-side (they arrive as serialized data, not as 'trusted' function arguments). Next.js adds CSRF protection by checking the origin (the Action-Submission-Origin / Next-Action headers) and the action ID, and it enforces that actions only run on the same-origin request. Because actions have access to server-only modules (database clients, secrets), an action that blindly accepts user data is the same class of vulnerability as an unvalidated API handler — the RPC sugar must not lull you into trusting client-supplied arguments.
interviewGotchas.trapWarning: The naive answer is 'actions are safe because they are server-side'. Server-side does not mean safe — it means privileged. The sharp answer walks through: CSRF/origin validation is built into the protocol, but authorization, rate limiting, and schema validation are still the developer's job. Another trap: claiming actions are not exposed as public endpoints — they are publicly reachable POST routes, which is why you must never rely on 'nobody will guess the action ID' as a security boundary.

interviewGotchas.question: How does a form action update the visible page without a client-side fetch?
interviewGotchas.contextIntro: This probes the RSC/flight payload mechanics behind the 'one round trip' claim — the interviewer wants the protocol, not just the DX.
interviewGotchas.detailedAnswer: When the form submits, the client sends a POST with the action ID and serialized FormData. The server runs the action, then builds a React Flight payload: it re-renders the affected server component tree (including any revalidatePath-triggered data refetches) and streams the serialized JSX back. The client parses the Flight stream and reconciles it into the existing React tree — patching only the parts that changed. Because the whole exchange uses React's serialization format, the UI updates and the server data stay consistent in a single request, and the navigation history is not polluted (unlike a redirect-and-refetch cycle).
interviewGotchas.trapWarning: A common wrong claim is 'the page fully reloads'. Form actions do not reload the page; they perform a background RPC and merge the returned Flight payload. Another trap: saying 'revalidatePath re-fetches on the client'. revalidatePath invalidates the Next.js data cache on the server; the refetch happens during the server-side re-render of the returned payload. Candidates who name the Flight payload and cache invalidation layers show they understand the architecture.
